title: Natural Language Processing
subtitle: Tokens, embeddings, and the architecture that ate the field

slides.title: This module IS how LLMs work
bullets: Module 04 is what happens when you SCALE what we build here
Do not skim this to reach LLMs faster -- you will pay for it
Pipeline: text -> tokens -> embeddings -> contextual vectors -> output
Everything in Modules 04 to 11 is this pipeline with a bigger middle
slides.notes: Set the stakes. The single most common mistake is rushing past the transformer to get to prompting.

slides.title: A compressed history
slides.notes: word2vec's king - man + woman = queen is the moment meaning became geometry.

slides.title: Tokenization: pick your granularity
slides.notes: BPE: start from bytes, repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair. That is the entire algorithm.

slides.title: Tokenization explains the weirdness
rows: it never sees letters, only chunks
vocab entries almost absent from training data
slides.notes: This table converts 'the model is dumb' into 'the tokenizer is lossy'. It changes how people debug.

slides.title: Count tokens with the model's own tokenizer
slides.quote: len(text)/4 is a guess, not a measurement.
bullets: English prose: roughly 1.3 tokens per word -- but measure
Code, JSON and other languages break the rule of thumb
Token count drives cost, latency and context limits
Build one yourself: code/bpe_tokenizer.py

slides.title: Embeddings: static vs contextual
bullets: Static (word2vec): one vector per word; 'bank' is a compromise
Contextual (BERT, GPT): the vector depends on the whole sequence
That shift is the biggest single quality jump in NLP history
Sentence embeddings are trained CONTRASTIVELY, not by averaging
Normalize vectors -> cosine similarity becomes a dot product
slides.notes: Flag the instruction-prefix trap: 'query:' vs 'passage:' silently wrecks retrieval if you get it wrong. Module 08.

slides.title: The Transformer
slides.subtitle: Drop the recurrence. Keep the attention.
slides.notes: Slow down here. Everything after this slide is the core of the course.

slides.title: The problem it solved
bullets: RNNs process one step at a time: no parallelism across time
Position 1's influence on position 1000 survives 999 sequential updates
2017: drop recurrence entirely, keep only attention
Every position attends to every other in ONE parallel op
The price: attention is O(n^2). Long context = paying less of that price

slides.title: Scaled dot-product attention
bullets: Query: what am I looking for? Key: what do I offer?
Value: what do I contribute if selected?
Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d_k)) V
It is a SOFT dictionary lookup -- a weighted blend, differentiable
scores -> scale -> mask -> softmax -> weighted sum of values
slides.notes: Ask them to explain Q, K, V without using the word 'attention'. It exposes who actually gets it.

slides.title: Why divide by sqrt(d_k)
slides.quote: Q.K sums d_k products, so its variance grows as d_k. Big logits saturate softmax and the gradient dies.
bullets: Unscaled: max weight -> 1.0, entropy -> 0, gradient p(1-p) -> 0
Scaled: std stays ~1 at every dimension
The most-asked transformer interview question
Know the VARIANCE argument, not just the formula

slides.title: Multi-head variants exist for ONE reason: inference memory
rows: shrinks KV cache; some quality loss
slides.notes: Not accuracy. Memory. The KV cache is what caps your batch size in production.

slides.title: The causal mask
bullets: Position i may attend only to positions <= i
Add -inf to scores BEFORE softmax, not zero weights after
Zeroing after softmax breaks the sum-to-1 property
This is what lets a decoder train on ALL positions in parallel
Also mask padding -- forgetting it is silent and degrades quality

slides.title: The transformer block (Pre-LN)
bullets: h   = x + MHA(LayerNorm(x))        <- residual 1
out = h + FFN(LayerNorm(h))        <- residual 2
FFN is per-position, d_ff = 4 * d_model, and holds ~2/3 of parameters
Post-LN (2017) needed careful warmup; Pre-LN is stable -- everyone moved
Llama-class models swap LayerNorm for the cheaper RMSNorm
slides.notes: Have them draw this from memory. If they cannot place the residuals, they cannot read a model card.

slides.title: Positional encoding: attention is order-blind
rows: rotate Q and K by angle m*theta
slides.notes: RoPE makes attention depend on relative position for free. Extending context = manipulating RoPE frequencies (YaRN, NTK scaling).

slides.title: The three families
slides.notes: Decoder-only won: one objective, parallel training, in-context learning for free. Encoders are NOT obsolete -- they are the cheap tool for embeddings and high-volume classification.

slides.title: The KV cache dominates inference economics
bullets: cache = 2 * layers * kv_heads * d_head * seq * batch * bytes
8B GQA model, 32k context, batch 16 -> ~69 GB of cache alone
Prefill is compute-bound and parallel; decode is bandwidth-bound and serial
KV cache, not weight count, caps your concurrency
Hence GQA, PagedAttention (vLLM), and prompt caching APIs
slides.notes: This slide is the bridge from architecture to your infrastructure bill.

slides.title: Efficiency techniques worth knowing by name
bullets: FlashAttention -- exact attention, tiled, never materialises the n x n matrix
Sliding-window / local attention -- Mistral, Longformer
Linear attention and SSMs -- Mamba, RWKV; increasingly hybrid stacks
Mixture-of-Experts -- route each token to k of N expert FFNs
At B=8, h=32, n=8192 the attention matrix is ~34 GB for ONE layer
slides.notes: FlashAttention is not an approximation. Same math, different memory choreography.

slides.title: Exit check
bullets: Explain Q, K, V without saying 'attention'
Justify sqrt(d_k) with the variance argument
Draw a Pre-LN block, residuals in the right places
Compute a KV cache size from a config, from memory
